{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YJhCco9w9LU "Meet Dr. Mary-Claire King, Ground-Breaking Geneticist and Tireless Human Rights Activist"], [[World Science Festival]], March 5, 2014 | video2 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tOP5pUIYhv4 "The Moth Presents Dr. Mary-Claire King at the World Science Festival"], [[The Moth]] at the World Science Festival, June 27, 2014}}

'''Mary-Claire King''' (born February 27, 1946)<ref name="Yount">{{cite book|chapter=Mary-Claire King|last1=Yount|first1=Lisa|title=A to Z of women in science and math|date=2008|publisher=Facts On File|location=New York|isbn=978-0-8160-6695-7|pages=153–156|chapter-url=https://www.mobt3ath.com/uplode/book/book-24728.pdf}}</ref> is an American [[geneticist]]. She was the first to show that [[breast cancer]] can be inherited due to mutations in the gene she called ''[[BRCA1]]''. She studies [[human genetics]] and is particularly interested in [[genetic heterogeneity]] and [[complex traits]].<ref name="UW">{{cite web |title=Mary-Claire King Professor of Genome Sciences and of Medicine (Medical Genetics) |url=http://www.gs.washington.edu/faculty/king.htm |website=UW Genome Sciences |access-date=12 February 2019}}</ref> She studies the interaction of genetics and environmental influences and their effects on human conditions such as breast and [[ovarian cancer]], inherited [[deafness]], [[schizophrenia]],<ref name="Angier" /> [[HIV]],  [[systemic lupus erythematosus]] and [[rheumatoid arthritis]].<ref name="Bock">{{cite news |last1=Bock |first1=Paula |title=The plan of all plans: Mary-Claire King and her team explore secrets of DNA |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/pacific-nw-magazine/the-plan-of-all-plans-mary-claire-king-and-her-team-explore-secrets-of-dna/ |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=Pacific NW Magazine |date=May 19, 2016}}</ref> She has been the [[American Cancer Society]] Professor of the Department of Genome Sciences and of Medical Genetics at the [[University of Washington School of Medicine]] since 1995.<ref name="Washington" />

Besides known for her accomplishment in identifying breast cancer genes, King is also known for demonstrating that humans and [[Common chimpanzee|chimpanzees]] are 99% genetically identical and for applying [[DNA sequencing|genomic sequencing]] to identify victims of [[human rights abuses]]. In 1984, in Argentina, she began working in identifying children who had been stolen from their families and adopted illegally under the military dictatorship during the [[Dirty War]] (1976–1983). She has received many awards, including the [[Lasker Award]] and the [[National Medal of Science]]. In 2002, ''[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]'' magazine recognized King  as one of the 50 most important women in science.<ref name="Svitil">{{cite news|last1=Svitil|first1=Kathy|title=The 50 Most Important Women in Science|url=http://discovermagazine.com/2002/nov/feat50/|access-date=21 December 2014|publisher=Discover|date=13 November 2002}}</ref>

==Early life==
Mary-Claire King was born on  February 27, 1946, to Harvey and Clarice King of [[Wilmette, Illinois]], near [[Chicago]]. Her father  worked for [[Standard Oil of Indiana]].<ref name="Yount"/>
When King was 15 years old, her childhood best friend died of cancer. King became interested in science in the hope of learning enough to prevent and treat such illnesses.<ref name="Dreifus"/>

==Education==
King received her undergraduate degree in mathematics (''cum laude'') from [[Carleton College]],  [[Phi Beta Kappa]],  in 1967.<ref name="Phi67">{{cite web |title=Life and Science |url=https://apps.carleton.edu/voice/?story_id=1313651&issue_id=1312881 |website=Carleton College Voice |access-date=18 February 2019|date=2015}}</ref><ref name="Carleton">{{cite web |title=Distinguished Achievement Award Mary-Claire King |url=https://apps.carleton.edu/alumni/classes/1967/assets/Mary_Claire_King_achievement_award.pdf |website=Carleton College |access-date=12 February 2019}}</ref>

King was accepted into the graduate program at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and soon became politically active. She helped to organize protests against U.S. involvement in the [[Vietnam War]] in 1970. She says: "The single most effective thing we did was on the day after the US invaded Cambodia, we got out our suit jackets and shirtwaist dresses – not clothes that any of us had worn since coming to Berkeley – and went to the synagogues and churches and by the end of Sunday we had 30,000 letters opposing the action."<ref name="Jaffe">{{cite journal|last1=Jaffe|first1=Sam|title=Mary-Claire King|journal=The Scientist|date=March 15, 2004|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/15482/title/Mary-Claire-King/|access-date=29 November 2016}}</ref>
She dropped out of university briefly after the [[National Guard]] was sent in against student protestors.<ref name="Zhu"/><ref name="KNAW"/>

She spent a year doing consumer advocacy work for [[Ralph Nader]], investigating pesticide use and its effects on farm workers.<ref name="Zhu">{{cite web |last1=Zhu |first1=Meilin |title=Mary-Claire King (1946– ) |url=https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/mary-claire-king-1946 |website=The Embryo Project Encyclopedia |access-date=12 February 2019|date=2017-08-23}}</ref><ref name="KNAW"/>

After her return to Berkeley, advisor [[Allan Wilson (biologist)|Allan Wilson]] persuaded her to switch from mathematics to genetics.<ref name="Elliott"/> King had been introduced to genetics by professor [[Curt Stern]], in the last class he taught before his retirement.<ref name="ShawBio">{{cite web |title=Autobiography of Mary-Claire King |url=http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=106&threeid=280&fourid=569&fiveid=256 |website=The Shaw Prize |access-date=12 February 2019 |archive-date=13 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190213005734/http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=106&threeid=280&fourid=569&fiveid=256 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
In her doctoral work at Berkeley, King demonstrated through comparative protein analysis that [[Common chimpanzee|chimpanzees]] and humans were 99% genetically identical. King's work supported Allan Wilson's view that chimpanzees and humans diverged only five million years ago, and King and Wilson suggested that [[gene regulation]] was likely responsible for the significant differences between the species.<ref>{{Cite journal

Next King went to [[Santiago, Chile]] to teach at the [[Universidad de Chile]] as part of a University of California-University of Chile exchange program. Her time there was cut short when the Chilean government of [[Salvador Allende]] was overthrown in a [[CIA]]-backed [[1973 Chilean coup d'état|military coup]] on September 11, 1973. King and her husband Robert Colwell returned to Berkeley in late December.<ref name="Elliott"/><ref name="BCRF">{{cite web |title=Q&A With Dr. Mary-Claire King |url=https://www.bcrf.org/qa-dr-mary-claire-king |website=Breast Cancer Research Foundation (BCRF) |access-date=12 February 2019|date=July 7, 2014}}</ref>
She later learned that a number of her colleagues and students had either disappeared or been killed.<ref name="Katholieke"/>

King accepted a postdoctoral position at the [[University of California, San Francisco]] (UCSF), to work with [[Nicholas L. Petrakis]]. As of January 1, 1974, King began to work on the problem of why breast cancer tends to appear in families.<ref name="BCRF"/><ref name="Elliott">{{cite web |last1=Elliott |first1=Ellen |title=Women in Science: Mary-Claire King |url=https://www.jax.org/news-and-insights/jax-blog/2017/february/mary-claire-king |website=The Jackson Laboratory |access-date=12 February 2019 |archive-date=14 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210214011527/https://www.jax.org/news-and-insights/jax-blog/2017/february/mary-claire-king |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Family==
King's younger brother Paul King, a mathematician and business consultant, was the CEO of Vanalco in [[Vancouver, Washington]].<ref name="McHale">{{cite news|last1=McHale|first1=Laurie|title=Putting the Puzzle Together|url=http://www.washington.edu/alumni/columns/sept96/king2.html|access-date=29 November 2016|work=Columns: The University of Washington Alumni Magazine|date=1996}}</ref>

King married ecologist Robert K. Colwell in 1973.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://viceroy.colorado.edu/Colwell|title=Robert K. Colwell Homepage|access-date=2019-05-01|archive-date=2022-02-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220222132111/http://viceroy.colorado.edu/colwell/|url-status=dead}}</ref> They have one child.<ref name="Entine">{{cite book |last1=Entine |first1=Jon |title=Abraham's children : race, identity, and the DNA of the chosen people |date=2007 |publisher=Grand Central Pub |location=New York |isbn=978-0-446-58063-2 |pages=270–289 |edition=1st |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_uO2jMwZVykC&pg=PT202 |access-date=13 February 2019}}</ref>  King and Colwell divorced in 1983.

==Career==
King accepted a faculty appointment at the University of California, Berkeley, as professor of genetics and epidemiology in 1976. She remained at UC Berkeley until 1995, when she accepted an appointment as the [[American Cancer Society]] Professor at the [[University of Washington]].<ref name="Washington">{{cite web |title=Mary-Claire King, PhD |url=https://medgen.uw.edu/faculty/mary-claire-king-phd |website=Division of Medical Genetics, University of Washington |access-date=14 February 2019 |archive-date=19 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210219092305/https://medgen.uw.edu/faculty/mary-claire-king-phd |url-status=dead }}</ref> She also served on the Life Sciences jury for the [[Infosys Prize]] in 2015.

==Research==
===Breast cancer===
From 1974 to 1990, King carried out years of painstaking research, seeking a genetic marker, an identifiable piece of genetic material, that tended to accompany the presence of breast cancer in families.<ref name="Lemelson">{{cite web |title=Mary-Claire King Genetic Breast Cancer Detection |url=https://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/mary-claire-king |website=Lemelson-MIT Program |access-date=14 February 2019}}</ref> For much of that time, the predominant theory was that cancer was [[Virus|viral]].<ref name="Dreifus">{{cite news |last1=Dreifus |first1=Claudia |title=A Never-Ending Genetic Quest |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/02/10/science/mary-claire-kings-pioneering-gene-work-from-breast-cancer-to-human-rights.html |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=The New York Times |date=February 9, 2015}}</ref>  Most scientists disregarded or attacked her ideas. The idea that genetic patterns could be linked to the incidence of complex diseases was considered an unlikely long shot.<ref name="Entine"/>  Genetics had been recognized as significant in diseases with a simple genetic tie, such as [[Huntington's disease]], [[cystic fibrosis]], and [[sickle-cell anemia]], but researchers were skeptical about the usefulness of genetics in studying more common and complex diseases involving both multiple genetic factors and environmental influences. King sometimes worried that she was going down a blind alley in trying to study the interplay of genetics with a complex human disease.<ref name="Entine"/> 
 
Nonetheless, the search for the breast cancer susceptibility gene was moving forward with firm steps in King's lab and accelerating in the mid-1980s.  On the basis of a series of unselected breast cancer cases and their family history, in 1988, King's team published a genetic epidemiological model for breast cancer, demonstrating the theoretical existence of a major dominant gene that conferred a high degree of susceptibility to breast cancer in a subset of the population.  Applying this genetic penetrance model and using the genotyping technology available at the time, King's team evaluated more than 170 genetic markers, utilizing the gene mapping technique known as [[Genetic linkage|linkage analysis]]. When they in 1990 finally found a genetic  marker that showed strong evidence in a subset of families, King's group demonstrated that a single gene on [[chromosome 17]] could be linked to many breast and ovarian cancers, and that genetic heterogeneity was present in breast cancer etiology. A team member suggested that they reorganize their data by age of onset, as in the study cohort, the families in which members had developed cancer at a relatively young age tended to show stronger evidence of linkage to this locus. The idea was that early cases might be more likely to reflect a genetic component, in contrast to sporadic mutations that might occur at any age or even accrue over time. As many as 5–10% of all cases of breast cancer may be hereditary.<ref name="Batt"/><ref name="Lemelson"/><ref name="Hall">{{Cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=J.|last2=Lee|first2=M.|last3=Newman|first3=B.|last4=Morrow|first4=J.|last5=Anderson|first5=L.|last6=Huey|first6=B.|last7=King|first7=M.|year=1990|title=Linkage of early-onset familial breast cancer to chromosome 17q21|journal=Science|volume=250|issue=4988|pages=1684–1689|bibcode=1990Sci...250.1684H|doi=10.1126/science.2270482|pmid=2270482}}</ref>  In 1991 King officially named the gene [[BRCA1]].<ref name="Miki"/>
Her discovery paved the way for identification of the gene sequence. In September 1994, [[Myriad Genetics]] published a paper on the positional cloning of the sequence after a highly publicized "race" by groups of scientists.<ref name="Gold"/><ref name="Race">{{cite journal |last1=King |first1=M.-C. |title="The Race" to Clone BRCA1 |journal=Science |date=27 March 2014 |volume=343 |issue=6178 |pages=1462–1465 |doi=10.1126/science.1251900 |pmid=24675952 |bibcode=2014Sci...343.1462K |s2cid=206555895 }}</ref><ref name="Miki">{{cite journal |last1=Miki |first1=Y |last2=Swensen |first2=J |last3=Shattuck-Eidens |first3=D |last4=Futreal |first4=P. |last5=Harshman |first5=K |last6=Tavtigian |first6=S |last7=Liu |first7=Q |last8=Cochran |first8=C |last9=Bennett |first9=L. |last10=Ding |first10=W |last11=et |first11=al. |title=A strong candidate for the breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility gene BRCA1 |journal=Science |date=7 October 1994 |volume=266 |issue=5182 |pages=66–71 |doi=10.1126/science.7545954|pmid=7545954 |bibcode=1994Sci...266...66M |doi-access=free }}</ref> In December 1994, King and her collaborators published results based on a second cohort of families.<ref name="Race"/><ref name="Friedman">{{cite journal |last1=Friedman |first1=Lori S. |last2=Ostermeyer |first2=Elizabeth A. |last3=Szabo |first3=Csilla I. |last4=Dowd |first4=Patrick |last5=Lynch |first5=Eric D. |last6=Rowell |first6=Sarah E. |last7=King |first7=Mary-Claire |title=Confirmation of BRCA1 by analysis of germline mutations linked to breast and ovarian cancer in ten families |journal=Nature Genetics |date=December 1994 |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=399–404 |doi=10.1038/ng1294-399 |pmid=7894493 |s2cid=2863113 }}</ref>  A second gene, [[BRCA2]], was also found.<ref name="Gold">{{cite journal |last1=Gold |first1=E Richard |last2=Carbone |first2=Julia |title=Myriad Genetics: In the eye of the policy storm |journal=Genetics in Medicine |date=April 2010 |volume=12 |issue=4 Suppl |pages=S39–S70 |doi=10.1097/GIM.0b013e3181d72661 |pmid=20393310 |pmc=3037261 }}</ref> These two genes, BRCA1 and BRCA2, work to clean up cells in the body that have been harmed by things such as tobacco or just help clean the cells because they have aged. When these genes do not perform these functions, cells will grow and divide quickly, leading to some types of cancers.<ref>{{cite web |title=BRCA1 gene BRCA1, DNA repair associated |url=https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/gene/brca1/ |website=Genetics Home Reference |publisher=National Library of Medicine |access-date=1 May 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=BRCA: The Breast Cancer Gene |url=https://www.nationalbreastcancer.org/what-is-brca |website=National Breast Cancer Foundation |access-date=1 May 2019}}</ref> Both genes worked to suppress the development of cancer tumors, but certain types of genetic mutations could prevent them from doing so.<ref name="Batt">{{cite book |last1=Batt |first1=Sharon |title=Patient no more : the politics of breast cancer |date=2003 |publisher=Gynergy |isbn=978-0-921881-30-8 |pages=170–176 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GZY809r0PlUC&pg=PA176 |access-date=14 February 2019}}</ref>

In 1996, with support from the [[Breast Cancer Research Foundation]] (BCRF) Mary-Claire King and social worker Joan Marks began the [[New York Breast Cancer Study]], which definitively determined that incidence of breast and ovarian cancer was linked to inherited mutations of the genes BRCA1 and BRCA2.  The researchers studied women of [[Ashkenazi Jewish]] ancestry in New York, a group that was known to have a very high incidence of breast cancer (up to an 80% risk by age 70, compared with 12% in the general population).<ref name="Landmark">{{cite news |title=Landmark study offers new information about breast cancer genes Helps participants understand options |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2003-10/slc-lso102203.php |access-date=14 February 2019 |work=EurekaAlert |publisher=Sarah Lawrence College |date=23 October 2003 |archive-date=14 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214174346/https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2003-10/slc-lso102203.php |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="King2003">{{cite journal |last1=King |first1=M.-C. |title=Breast and Ovarian Cancer Risks Due to Inherited Mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 |journal=Science |date=24 October 2003 |volume=302 |issue=5645 |pages=643–646 |doi=10.1126/science.1088759 |pmid=14576434 |bibcode=2003Sci...302..643K |s2cid=33441900 }}</ref> She has also studied the incidence of breast cancer in Palestinian women.<ref name="Lolas Hamameh">{{cite journal |last1=Lolas Hamameh |first1=Suhair |last2=Renbaum |first2=Paul |last3=Kamal |first3=Lara |last4=Dweik |first4=Dima |last5=Salahat |first5=Mohammad |last6=Jaraysa |first6=Tamara |last7=Abu Rayyan |first7=Amal |last8=Casadei |first8=Silvia |last9=Mandell |first9=Jessica B. |last10=Gulsuner |first10=Suleyman |last11=Lee |first11=Ming K. |last12=Walsh |first12=Tom |last13=King |first13=Mary-Claire |last14=Levy-Lahad |first14=Ephrat |last15=Kanaan |first15=Moein |title=Genomic analysis of inherited breast cancer among Palestinian women: Genetic heterogeneity and a founder mutation in TP53 |journal=International Journal of Cancer |date=15 August 2017 |volume=141 |issue=4 |pages=750–756 |doi=10.1002/ijc.30771 |pmid=28486781 |pmc=5526459 }}</ref>

The discovery of the "breast cancer gene" revolutionized the study of numerous other diseases and phenotypes. The model and technique King developed to identify BRCA1 has since proven valuable in the study of many other illnesses and conditions.<ref name="BCRF"/> King's contributions have made it possible for people to be informed of genetic information that then can aid them in making choices best for themselves and for their future.<ref name="Shute">{{cite news|last1=Shute|first1=Nancy|title=How Being Ignored Helped A Woman Discover the Breast Cancer Gene|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2014/03/27/295270360/how-being-ignored-helped-a-woman-discover-the-breast-cancer-gene|access-date=29 November 2016|work=All Things Considered|date=March 27, 2014}}</ref><ref name="Entine"/>

King also worked on a project studying the mutations of genes linked to breast cancer inheritance in Nigerian women between March 1998 and 2014. King's team decided to do this research on the grounds that more people die in Nigeria from triple negative breast cancer that is diagnosed at a later stage than other, more educated regions of the world, such as Europe or America. At the finish of this study, King's team was still unsure of the reason for such high levels of [[Triple-negative breast cancer]], since many of the people diagnosed were not showing mutations in the BRCA1 gene. Her study supported the idea that genomic sequencing could be useful as a tool to help detect gene mutations early and be proactive in letting those who have high risks for breast cancer know ahead of time.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zheng|first1=Yonglan|last2=Walsh|first2=Tom|last3=Gulsuner|first3=Suleyman|last4=Casadei|first4=Silvia|last5=Lee|first5=Ming K.|last6=Ogundiran|first6=Temidayo O.|last7=Ademola|first7=Adeyinka|last8=Falusi|first8=Adeyinka G.|last9=Adebamowo|first9=Clement A.|date=October 2018|title=Inherited Breast Cancer in Nigerian Women|journal=Journal of Clinical Oncology|volume=36|issue=28|pages=2820–2825|doi=10.1200/jco.2018.78.3977|pmid=30130155|pmc=6161833|issn=0732-183X}}</ref>

===Hearing loss and deafness===
Since 1990, King has been working in collaboration with scientists around the world to identify genetic causes of [[hearing loss]] and [[deafness]]. They localized the first [[nonsyndromic deafness]]-related gene, DFNA1, in a [[Costa Rica]] kindred,<ref name="Lynch">{{cite journal |last1=Lynch |first1=E. D. |title=Nonsyndromic Deafness DFNA1 Associated with Mutation of a Human Homolog of the Drosophila Gene diaphanous |journal=Science |date=14 November 1997 |volume=278 |issue=5341 |pages=1315–1318 |doi=10.1126/science.278.5341.1315 |pmid=9360932 |bibcode=1997Sci...278.1315L }}</ref> and successfully cloned the gene in 1999.<ref>{{cite news |title=Pioneers of Science: Dr Mary-Claire King |page=21 |work=Research Media |url=http://www.internationalinnovation.com/build/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Pioneers_132_Exclusive_USAID_p2_Intl_Innovation_132_Research_Media.pdf |access-date=19 February 2019 |archive-date=24 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024054954/http://www.internationalinnovation.com/build/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Pioneers_132_Exclusive_USAID_p2_Intl_Innovation_132_Research_Media.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="DFNA1">{{cite journal |last1=King |first1=Mary-Claire |title=G DFNA1 in Inherited Hearing Loss |url=http://grantome.com/grant/NIH/R01-DC001076-10 |journal=Grantome |access-date=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref name="Nonsyndromic">{{cite web |title=Nonsyndromic hearing loss |url=https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/nonsyndromic-hearing-loss/ |website=Genetics Home Reference |publisher=U.S. National Library of Medicine |access-date=19 February 2019}}</ref>

King continues to work with scientists [[Karen Avraham]] at [[Tel Aviv University]] in [[Israel]] and [[Moien Kanaan]] at [[Bethlehem University]] in [[Palestine]], modeling international scientific cooperation in conjunction with conducting scientific research.  Hereditary deafness is common among some Palestinian and Israeli communities, providing good study populations to understand the genetics of this condition.<ref name="Mideast">{{cite news |title=Science transcends Mideast turmoil with geneticist's help |url=https://newsroom.uw.edu/postscript/science-transcends-mideast-turmoil-geneticists-help |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=UW Medicine Newsroom |publisher=University of Washington |date=April 30, 2018 |archive-date=26 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221226060842/https://newsroom.uw.edu/postscript/science-transcends-mideast-turmoil-geneticists-help |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Grantome">{{cite journal |last1=King |first1=Mary-Claire |title=Genetics of Hearing Loss in Palestinian Kindreds |url=http://grantome.com/grant/NIH/R03-TW001294-01 |journal=Grantome |access-date=19 February 2019}}</ref>

{{blockquote|We understand that working together transcends politics. It's possible to do beautiful useful science together, even between countries that are in conflict.|Mary-Claire King, 2018<ref name="Mideast"/>}}The genetic etiology of hearing loss is extremely heterogeneous, with a very high degree of complexity among Middle Eastern populations, presenting a different level of challenge for genetic analysis.  King's collaboration with scientists in Israel and Palestine has resolved the complex web of different genes and varying modes of transmission for this common phenotype among many kindreds in the communities in that region.

===Schizophrenia===
King in recent years has developed a deep interest in studying the genetic factors influencing [[schizophrenia]].   In collaboration with other scientists including [[Judith L. Rapoport]], [[Jonathan Sebat]], and [[Deborah L. Levy]], she has discovered evidence that suggests that schizophrenia may be linked to the presence of genetic mutations called [[copy-number variation|copy number variations]] (CNVs) in pathways involved in neural development. A percentage of such variations may occur spontaneously as a result of copying errors in cells.<ref name="Hamilton">{{cite news |last1=Hamilton |first1=Jonathan |title=Genetic Link to Schizophrenia Discovered |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=89163694 |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=All Things Considered |agency=NPR |date=March 27, 2008}}</ref><ref name="BB2010">{{cite news |title=Mary-Claire King and Judith Rapoport: New Hope From Discovery of Rare Genetic Mutations in Schizophrenia |url=https://www.bbrfoundation.org/content/mary-claire-king-and-judith-rapoport-new-hope-discovery-rare-genetic-mutations-schizophrenia |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=Brain and Behavior Research Foundation |date=April 1, 2010}}</ref><ref name="CSHL">{{cite news |title=CSHL scientists part of team that discovers role of rare gene mutations in schizophrenia |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2008-03/cshl-csp032808.php |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=EurekaAlert |date=28 March 2008}}</ref><ref name="Walsh">{{cite journal |last1=Walsh |first1=T. |last2=McClellan |first2=J. ===Human Genome Diversity Project===
King has also worked on the [[Human Genome Diversity Project]], led by [[Luca Cavalli-Sforza]].  The project seeks to delineate the distinctions among individuals in order to further understanding of human evolution and historical migrations.<ref name="Angier"/><ref name="Kreeger">{{cite news |last1=Kreeger |first1=Karen Young |title=Proposed Human Genome Diversity Project Still Plagued By Controversy And Questions |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/news/proposed-human-genome-diversity-project-still-plagued-by-controversy-and-questions-57807 |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=The Scientist |date=Oct 14, 1996 |archive-date=26 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190326010322/https://www.the-scientist.com/news/proposed-human-genome-diversity-project-still-plagued-by-controversy-and-questions-57807 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="GENOME">{{cite book |last1=United States. Congress. Senate. Committee on Governmental Affairs |title=Human Genome Diversity Project : hearing before the Committee on Governmental Affairs, United States Senate, One Hundred Third Congress, first session, April 26, 1993 |date=April 26, 1993 |publisher=U.S. G.P.O. |location=Washington |isbn=978-0-16-043334-4 |url=https://archive.org/details/humangenomediver00unit |access-date=19 February 2019}}</ref><ref name="Reardon">{{cite journal |last1=Reardon |first1=Jenny |title=The Human Genome Diversity Project: A Case Study in Coproduction |journal=Social Studies of Science |date=June 2001 |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=357–388 |doi=10.1177/030631201031003002 |s2cid=145626708 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Romanov exhumation===
King is well known for her work on the forensic determination of individual identity, in particular the use of mitochondrial DNA from teeth.<ref name="Ginther">{{cite journal |last1=Ginther |first1=Charles |last2=Issel-Tarver |first2=Laurie |last3=King |first3=Mary-Claire |title=Identifying individuals by sequencing mitochondrial DNA from teeth |journal=Nature Genetics |date=October 1992 |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=135–138 |doi=10.1038/ng1092-135 |pmid=1303263 |s2cid=28779140 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
King was invited to participate in DNA investigations of the first analysis of [[Execution of the Romanov family|Romanov remains]] exhumed in 1991 in [[Ekaterinburg]], Russia.<ref name="Ehrlich"/>

==Human rights work==
King first applied her genetics skills to human rights work in 1984, when she and her lab began working with [[Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo]] (Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo) in [[Argentina]]. She used dental genetics to identify missing persons, ultimately identifying 59 children and helping return them to their biological families. Most had been born to women in prison who had been persecuted as political dissidents and were later "disappeared" by the Argentine military [[Jorge Rafael Videla|dictatorship]] during the eight-year "[[Dirty War]]" from 1976 to 1983. These children were often illegally "adopted" by military families without their mother's or other family consent.<ref name="Dreifus"/><ref name="Angier">{{cite news |last1=Angier |first1=Natalie |title=SCIENTIST AT WORK: Mary-Claire King; Quest for Genes and Lost Children |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/04/27/science/scientist-at-work-mary-claire-king-quest-for-genes-and-lost-children.html?module=inline |access-date=19 February 2019 |work=The New York Times |date=April 27, 1993}}</ref>

Beginning in 1977 [[Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo|Las Abuelas]] ("the grandmothers") had gathered to protest the disappearance of their grandchildren and seek their return. Every Thursday, they marched to the central plaza in [[Buenos Aires]] ("[[Plaza de Mayo]]") to demand the return of their grandchildren, and they began gathering data trying to identify the many missing children (estimated to be 400–500).<ref name="Angier"/>

By the time King joined the project, the dictatorship had been replaced by a democratic government, but it required proof of kinship to remove children from families and return them to biological families. King's technique, using [[mitochondrial DNA]] and [[human leukocyte antigen]] serotyping genetic markers from dental samples, proved invaluable. The [[Supreme Court of Argentina]] in 1984 determined that King's test had positively identified the relationship of Paula Logares to her family, establishing the precedent for the ultimate reunification of dozens of families with their stolen children.<ref name="Nelson">{{cite news|first=Bryn|last= Nelson|title=Using genetics for human rights|url=http://www.dailyuw.com/news/article_228f727f-0415-52a0-bde3-53c62523cd99.html|access-date=29 November 2016|work=The Online Daily of the University of Washington|date=May 12, 1997}}</ref><ref name="Angier"/>

Since 1984, this technique has become a major method for genetic identification of the deceased as well as the living. In 1993 King used the technique to identify the remains of individuals massacred in the village of [[El Mozote]], [[El Salvador]]. More than 750 adults and children were massacred and buried in mass graves by US-trained Salvadoran soldiers<ref name="Angier"/> of the [[Atlácatl Battalion]].<ref name="Harvey-Blankenship">{{cite web |title= GENETIC TRACING, DISAPPEARED CHILDREN AND JUSTICE |author-first1=Michele |author-last1=Harvey-Blankenship |author-first2=Phuong N. |author-last2=Pham |author-first3=Rachel |author-last3=Shigekane |url=https://www.unicef-irc.org/publications/pdf/iwp_2010_12.pdf |access-date=12 February 2019 |website= UNICEF|publisher= Innocenti Research Centre |date=June 2010}}</ref>

King has worked with numerous human rights organizations, such as [[Physicians for Human Rights]] and [[Amnesty International]], to identify missing people in countries including Argentina,<ref name="Argentina">{{cite web |title=Partnerships: Scientists Working With Human Rights Organizations |url=https://www.aaas.org/programs/scientific-responsibility-human-rights-law/partnerships-scientists-working-human-rights-organizations |website=AAAS |access-date=19 February 2019}}</ref> Chile, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Mexico, Rwanda, the Balkans (Croatia and Serbia), and the Philippines.<ref name="Owens">{{cite journal |last1=Owens |first1=Kelly N |last2=Harvey-Blankenship |first2=Michelle |last3=King |first3=Mary-Claire |title=Genomic sequencing in the service of human rights |journal=International Journal of Epidemiology |date=February 2002 |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=53–58 |doi=10.1093/ije/31.1.53 |pmid=11914294 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=King |first1=MC |title=An application of DNA sequencing to a human rights problem. |journal=Molecular Genetic Medicine |date=1991 |volume=1 |pages=117–31 |pmid=1842570|doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-462001-8.50009-0 |isbn=978-0-12-462001-8 }}</ref> King's lab has also provided DNA identification for the U.S. Army,<ref>{{cite web |title=Mary-Claire King Professor of Genome Sciences and of Medicine (Medical Genetics) |url=https://www.gs.washington.edu/faculty/king.htm |access-date=19 February 2019 |website=UW Genome Sciences}}</ref> the United Nations,<ref name="Ball"/> and the U.N.'s [[war crimes]] tribunals.<ref name="Greengard"/>

King has been highly critical of genetic patenting, a practice which was ruled against by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2013, on the grounds that "genes are natural products and cannot be patented".<ref name="Dreifus"/><ref name="Schubert">{{Cite journal
| last1 = Schubert | first1 = Charlotte
| title = Profile: Mary-Claire King
| doi = 10.1038/nm0603-633
| journal = Nature Medicine
| volume = 9
| issue = 6
| page = 633
| year = 2003
| pmid = 12778148
| s2cid = 29601178
| doi-access = free
}}</ref>
